title: Different Ways to Add Parentheses
statement:
`expression` is a formula of non-negative whole numbers joined by the binary operators `+`, `-` and `*`. Each way of fully parenthesising it fixes the order in which its operators are applied. Evaluate the formula once for every distinct parenthesisation and return all of those values as a list. Two different groupings that happen to give the same value each contribute their own entry, so the list may contain repeats. A formula with no operator has exactly one grouping: the number itself. The values may be returned in any order.

The inputs guarantee that every value in the answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer and that the answer has at most 10^4 entries.
constraints: expression contains only digits and the characters '+', '-' and '*'
Every number in expression is between 0 and 99
Numbers have no sign of their own: '+' and '-' only appear as operators between two numbers
notes:
## Intuition

Every full parenthesisation has one operator that is applied last. Choosing that operator splits the formula into a left part and a right part, each of which can be grouped independently. So the values of the whole formula are exactly "every left value combined with every right value", taken over every possible last operator. The same sub-formula (for example `3-4`) shows up under many different splits, so caching each sub-formula's list of values avoids recomputing it.

## Approach

1. `solve(text)` returns every value of the sub-formula `text`; `memo` caches its answers by text.
2. Scan `text` for operators. For an operator at index `i`, recursively get `leftResults` for `text.slice(0, i)` and `rightResults` for `text.slice(i + 1)`.
3. Combine every `left` with every `right` using that operator and push the value into `results`.
4. If no operator was found, `text` is a single number: its only value is `Number(text)`.
5. Store `results` in `memo` and return it; the answer is `solve(expression)`.

## Example 1, step by step

For `"2-1-1"`, the first `-` (index 1) splits it into `"2"` and `"1-1"`. `"2"` gives `[2]`; `"1-1"` splits once into `[1]` and `[1]` and gives `[0]`, so this split adds `2 - 0 = 2`. The second `-` (index 3) splits into `"2-1"` (values `[1]`) and `"1"` (values `[1]`), adding `1 - 1 = 0`. The result is `[2, 0]`, which matches `[0, 2]` in any order.

## Complexity

- Time: proportional to the size of the output, which grows like the Catalan number C(n-1) for n numbers (4,862 for 10 numbers); memoisation keeps each sub-formula's list built only once.
- Space: the same order, for the cached lists of every sub-formula plus the recursion depth of at most n.

## Pitfalls

- Do not remove duplicates: two groupings with equal values are two separate entries (Example 2 has `-10` twice).
- Numbers can have two digits, so parse the whole operand (`Number(text)`), not a single character.
- The base case is "no operator found", not "length 1": `"99"` is a single number.
- Apply `-` as `left - right`; the order of the operands matters.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `memo` | cache from a sub-formula's text to its list of values |
| `text` | the sub-formula `solve` is currently evaluating |
| `results` | every value found for `text` |
| `i`, `op` | position and character of the operator tried as the last one applied |
| `leftResults`, `rightResults` | all values of the parts left and right of `op` |
| `left`, `right` | one value from each side being combined |
